events.text: Day 1 begins.

We have no evidence yet, so I’d be cautious about forcing a Day 1 elimination. Five votes are needed, and roles won’t be revealed on death, so let’s make our reasoning and votes clear rather than treating a consensus as proof.

I agree with the caution Arjun expressed. With nine players alive, two mafia hidden among us, and no role reveals on death, a Day 1 elimination is a real gamble — we'd be removing one of five possible town power players or villagers with essentially zero information, and it costs us five votes of coordination we don't have evidence to support. For me, the most useful thing today isn't finding someone to eliminate; it's building a baseline. I'd ask everyone to pay attention not just to what people say, but how they say it — who pushes hard for a lynch without offering reasoning, who stays vague, who quietly piles onto a wagon only after it forms. Those patterns won't convict anyone today, but they'll matter a lot tomorrow after the night gives us a death to work with. I also want to flag the vote math: we need at least five votes to eliminate anyone, which means a coalition, which means whoever forms that coalition will be visible to the mafia. I'd rather we spend today talking about how we want to handle voting when the time comes — do we want to demand a claim or reasoning before confirming any lynch, even a soft one? My instinct is yes: no elimination on Day 1 unless someone genuinely earns five votes with real substance, and I'd personally be comfortable with a no-elimination day if nothing develops. That preserves numbers, and numbers are the town's only real resource against two coordinated killers. That's my position for now — I'm listening more than accusing at this point.

I want to come out on the same side as Lucia here, and I'll add my own reasoning rather than just agreeing.

With nine alive, two killers, and no role reveals, an elimination today is not a free action — it's a coin flip on which of five power players we're removing, and a coin flip on which of the two hidden killers we're removing. Even in the good case we learn one name. In the bad case we've handed the mafia their cleanest night: fewer town players, no information about who's left, and the chance that the person we lynched was the detective or the doctor.

I also think the sequencing matters more than the vote. If we lynch on Day 1 with no claims and no accusations, then tonight the mafia picks their target, and tomorrow we wake up with one death and one elimination's worth of silence. That is the worst possible setup for the town — we will have burned a day and a body with nothing to reason from.

So my position is a no-elimination day unless someone earns five votes with actual substance behind them. I want to be honest that this feels uncomfortable, because "no elimination" can look like a stall, and it can be abused by the killers. That's exactly why Lucia's suggestion is the right one: define the standard in advance. If we're going to wait, we should agree now on what we'll accept later — a claim, a contradiction, a failed police report, an unexplained vote. Fixing the bar now protects us from the mafia being the only side that benefits from vagueness.

One small caution. Baseline-building is fine, but silence is also a choice, and the people who have said least so far are the ones we know least about. Omar, you've been quiet — that's not an accusation, but it does mean right now you have the least to lose by speaking plainly. Everyone who wants to wait for evidence should be willing to give some, starting with themselves.

I'll vote to abstain today if nobody puts forward a case worth acting on.

Thanks for the nudge, Felix, though to be fair, only three people had spoken before me, so it was just poll timing rather than intentional silence. On the substance of the discussion, I understand the hesitation around a Day 1 elimination given the nine-player count and lack of role reveals. Nobody wants to accidentally eliminate a town power role or hand mafia an easy numbers advantage. However, I want to push back slightly against locking ourselves into a no-elimination mindset this early. If the mafia senses that town is predetermined to abstain unless some unattainable bar of evidence is cleared, they have no reason to sweat, take risky stances, or expose themselves. The town's primary information generator on Day 1 is pressure, watching who pushes wagons, who hesitates, and how people react when they are under scrutiny. We do not have to commit to lynching blindly, but we should actively question each other, test theories, and see how everyone responds before defaulting to a pass. If we simply agree to do nothing, we give the mafia an uncontested night kill while gaining minimal behavioral data. I would like to see the rest of the group speak up so we have actual substance across the board.

I’m Leo. I agree with the caution about not forcing a blind Day 1 elimination, but I also think Omar is right that we shouldn’t pre-commit so hard to abstaining that the mafia can coast. My position: no lynch unless someone actually earns five votes with a real case — a contradiction, an unexplained wagon, or a claim that doesn’t hold up. Until then, I’m willing to abstain, but I want us to use today to create pressure and a behavioral baseline. I’m not accusing anyone yet. Priya, you haven’t spoken yet: do you support treating Day 1 as a default no-elimination, or do you want us to actively pressure someone with votes today? Please answer that specifically.

Leo, to answer you directly: I support a default no-elimination on Day 1. I have no evidence pointing at anyone, and a lynch today would remove one of seven town players with nothing to learn from it. I don't want silence to be the default either, though. I'd support agreeing now on a bar: anyone who wants a vote on a player should cite something specific said in this thread, and everyone should say plainly where they stand on that player. Omar, you argued that pressure is town's main information source. Concretely, what would you need to see today before you put a vote on someone, and would you vote on a player with less than that? I'd like to know whether we disagree about the bar itself or about whether a bar should exist at all.

Priya, to answer you directly: we definitely do not disagree about whether a bar should exist. I would never advocate voting someone out carelessly or without cause, especially on Day 1 with no role reveals.

To be concrete about what I would need to see before casting an elimination vote:
1. A clear contradiction or inconsistency in someone's reasoning when pressed.
2. Opportunistic behavior, such as a player quietly slipping onto a forming wagon with borrowed or superficial logic.
3. Blatant evasion or refusal to state clear stances when directly addressed.

Would I vote with less than that? No. If we engage everyone and nobody exhibits that kind of anti-town behavior, I am entirely comfortable voting to abstain. My earlier point was simply that treating no-elimination as a pre-ordained conclusion before the day even gets going removes any incentive for the mafia to take risks or speak carefully. Pressure is a diagnostic tool to evaluate reactions, even if it ends without an execution.

We still have not heard from Sam, Maya, or Isha. Seeing where everyone stands and how people engage when prompted will give us much better material to judge.

I’m Sam. I’m cautious about an elimination without a real case, but I agree with Omar that we should test people’s reasoning rather than settle the outcome in advance.

Priya, you said a lynch today would remove one of seven town players. That isn’t certain: it could also eliminate a mafia player, though we have no reliable basis to pick one yet. Does that correction change your view of the tradeoff?

Sam, fair correction, and it's a good one. A lynch could hit a mafia player, and I shouldn't have framed it as certainly removing a town player. Still, with no information, a random living player is town 7 times out of 9, so a blind Day 1 lynch most likely removes a town player and gives us nothing to reason from. That keeps my position. Your correction shows the trade is a gamble, not a sure loss, but it's still a bad gamble today.

Omar, your three criteria are close to what I'd accept, and I'd add one requirement: anyone casting a vote should cite a specific quote or moment from this thread. Opportunistic behavior is hard to judge on Day 1 unless someone points to the exact moment, and that keeps the bar concrete for everyone, including the accuser.

My stance for today: no elimination unless someone meets that bar. I'm not accusing anyone yet, and I'll vote to abstain if nobody brings a case with specifics.

Maya, you haven't spoken yet. Do you support a default no-elimination on Day 1, or do you want us to pressure someone with votes today? Please answer that directly.

Maya here. Priya, thanks for asking directly — yes, I support a default no-elimination on Day 1. I have no specific reason to suspect anyone, and a blind lynch statistically favors removing a town player. But I also agree with Omar and Leo that we shouldn't treat abstention as a settled outcome before the day is over.

Here's where I land: I want us to hold ourselves to the bar Priya and Omar have outlined — cite a specific quote or moment before pushing a wagon, and don't let anyone slide onto a vote without justification. That bar protects the town from sloppy play while still leaving room for pressure.

One observation from the discussion so far: several players (Arjun, Lucia, Felix, Priya, Omar, Leo, Sam) have all weighed in on the Day 1 strategy question, and mostly we're converging on the same position — no blind lynch, build a baseline, set the standard now. That consensus is fine, but I want to flag that unanimity itself can be comfortable for the mafia. If all seven of us who've spoken agree that nothing happens today, then two players are hiding behind that agreement with zero cost.

So my ask is this: Isha, you're the only player besides me who hasn't spoken yet. When you do speak, tell us something beyond the Day 1 strategy question — is there anyone's reasoning so far you've found suspicious, inconsistent, or overly eager? Even a weak read is more useful to us right now than another agreement. The two mafia players are sitting in this thread absorbing everyone's thought process for free; the least we can do is make them earn their silence by expecting specific reactions from everyone.

Maya, my weakest concern is Felix’s nudge to Omar for being quiet when only three players had spoken. That treated poll timing as a reason to scrutinize him, though Felix did say it wasn’t an accusation. It’s not enough for an elimination case, but it stood out to me.

Felix, what did you hope to learn from singling Omar out at that point, rather than asking the group for responses?

More broadly, I’m against a blind elimination, but I don’t think abstention should be automatic. Specific questions and public reasoning now can give us something to compare with later votes and claims.

Isha, direct answer: I wasn't running a targeted scan, and my call-out was genuinely sloppy reasoning on my part. I had three turns of context, saw the poll pass to a player who hadn't spoken, and filled the gap with a nudge instead of simply waiting for the roster to fill in. Omar corrected that in his next speech, and the correction was fair — I described it as an accusation when it was a timing artifact. I'll own that.

What I *hoped* to learn was narrow and, in hindsight, not worth the framing: I wanted to know whether someone who hadn't spoken would engage with a direct address or would stay silent, because silence that persists under a question is a data point. But I applied that lens asymmetrically — to whoever happened to be quiet — and I did it to the wrong target at the wrong moment. If you want to be fair to me, note that I've now spoken at length, twice, and given up more of my own reasoning than anyone else here, so the 'quiet player' pattern doesn't apply to me anymore.

If it helps, here's my full position so nothing is hidden: I support a no-elimination Day 1, but I don't support a *pre-committed* one. I said the bar should be fixed in advance — a claim, a contradiction, a failed police report, an unexplained vote — and I'm the one who argued most specifically that silence is a choice and the people who have said least are the ones we know least about. That argument cuts against me, and I'll take it. If someone wants to use my nudge to read me, that's a legitimate read and I'd rather have it on the record now than have it used against me later.

The part I'd push back on isn't the scrutiny of my nudge — it's the pattern in the room: seven players have converged on the same procedural position without once naming a specific moment that anyone said. That's convenient for two people who are reading this thread right now. Omar, you're the one player who explicitly pushed back on pre-committing to abstention, and your criteria are notably elastic — 'opportunistic behavior' and 'blatant evasion' could be stretched to fit almost anyone who isn't eager to lynch. Isha, given my answer, does my nudge still look like a targeted scan to you, or was it what Omar called it — poll timing?

Felix, I didn’t call your nudge a targeted scan. My concern was that you treated Omar’s lack of speech as meaningful when poll timing was a sufficient explanation. Your admission that the framing was sloppy is reasonable, and I don’t think it warrants an elimination by itself.

One other point: you say seven players converged without naming a specific moment, but I had just named your nudge, and Sam had specifically challenged Priya’s statement about a lynch necessarily hitting town. That overstatement is worth noting, though it could simply be a mistake.

For now, Felix remains a weak concern, not a case I’d vote on. I’m still opposed to a blind elimination and open to revisiting that if a stronger, specific case emerges.

Two turns of my own reasoning on the record now, so let me put my position cleanly and try to close this day the way I actually think it should end.

Where I land: I support the standard we keep converging on — no elimination today unless a specific, citable moment is named. I want to add one honest caveat to my own earlier framing. I said the sequencing of a Day 1 lynch followed by a night kill would be the worst setup for the town. That was too confident. In practice a Day 1 lynch is a gamble with a 2-in-9 chance of removing a killer outright, so the real cost is that a wrong lynch plus a night death leaves us with two bodies and no reliable information. My point stands, but I should have said "a likely wrong lynch" instead of implying every outcome is bad. Sam's correction on the 7-of-9 town math was right and I want to be clear I'm not arguing with it.

Why the bar protects me as much as it protects the town: I have no case against anyone. The nudge at Omar was sloppy, and Isha's read of it was fair — I applied a silence lens to whoever happened to be quiet rather than to the roster as a whole. The fix for that isn't a vote, it's a commitment to citing specifics, and I'm making it: if I ever put a vote on someone, I will quote the exact sentence they said and name the inconsistency. If I can't do that, I won't vote for them, and I'll say so.

I also want to be straightforward about something rather than let it sit in the background. There are two killers in this room and they have heard every strategic position stated in detail today. A standard that requires citable specifics is genuinely the strongest tool we have against them, because they have to produce content too, and content is checkable. A standard built on "vague feel" or "who is being too eager" is much easier for a killer to satisfy by simply sounding measured and helpful. So I'd rather we have a boring, concrete bar than a dramatic one.

Maya, you were the one who said unanimity itself can be comfortable for the mafia, and that you wanted to see specific reactions rather than another strategy agreement. That's the sharpest thing anyone has said today. So let me ask you directly and specifically: do you have a particular moment from anyone's speech above that meets the bar you just endorsed — a specific quote, a stated stance that contradicts something else they said, or a refusal to answer a direct question? If you have one, name it and I'll consider it seriously rather than dismiss it as thin. If you don't, then I'll take your own point seriously and support abstaining rather than manufacturing a case to avoid looking cautious.

Felix, direct answer to your question: yes, I have two specific moments that meet the bar — both are weak individually, but they're real and citable.

First: Priya said a Day 1 lynch would remove "one of seven town players," and Sam correctly pointed out that's not certain — it could hit mafia. Priya acknowledged the correction. That's a specific, named moment where a stated position was overstated and then walked back. It's not scummy, but it meets the citation bar.

Second: you, Felix, flagged that Omar's criteria — "opportunistic behavior" and "blatant evasion" — are elastic enough to fit almost anyone. Omar then accepted Priya's additional requirement of citing exact quotes, which partially addresses your concern, but the original framing he offered first was loose. When Priya pressed him with a concrete question about what he'd need to see, he gave a reasonable answer — but that answer came only after direct questioning, not volunteered upfront. That pattern of giving sharper positions only under pressure is worth remembering.

That said, neither moment is close to five votes, and I wouldn't push either as an elimination case. My honest read is that this thread has been almost entirely procedural, which means the two killers have been studying us for free while contributing nothing risky. The unanimity concern I raised earlier still stands.

I support abstention today unless someone breaks pattern. My ask to the group going forward: tomorrow, when we have a night death to reason from, let's commit to naming specific moments from the start rather than debating process. The killers are excellent at process debate — it's how they hide.

Maya, one correction: Omar hasn’t responded since Priya added the exact-quote requirement, so we can’t say he accepted it. His three criteria were also offered in direct response to Priya’s question; I’m not sure sharpening them under questioning is suspicious by itself.

Felix’s early nudge remains a weak concern for me, but he acknowledged the timing problem. I don’t see a case strong enough to vote for an elimination today. Tomorrow, a night death may provide context, but it won’t reveal the victim’s role, so we should avoid treating it as confirmation of anyone’s alignment.

Sam, fair catch on Omar — he hasn't responded to Priya's exact-quote requirement yet, and I shouldn't have implied he accepted it. That's a good reminder of why precision matters in what we cite.

A few things as the day winds down. Felix has used all three of his speaking turns, so his positions are locked: he supports abstention, committed to citing specific quotes before voting, and owns the Omar nudge as sloppy framing. That's on the record for the voting phase.

The bar we've converged on — cite a specific moment before pushing a wagon — has already proven its worth. Sam corrected me twice today: first on the lynch math, then on Omar's silence. Both corrections made my claims sharper. That's the process working.

On the two weak concerns I raised earlier: Priya's overstated claim and Omar's elastic criteria — Sam's pushback on the second one is a fair point that Omar offered his criteria in direct response to a question. Neither concern is close to five votes, and I wouldn't push either as a case. I'll abstain today unless something specific breaks pattern.

My honest read on the room: the discussion has been thoughtful and the bar-setting is sound, but almost all of it has been procedural. Nobody has said anything risky. That's expected on Day 1, but it means tomorrow we need to shift to substance — the night death gives us a name to work with even if it doesn't reveal a role.

Lucia, you opened the day with the strongest framework: watch how people speak, not just what they say. After everything since — Felix's nudge and walk-back, Priya's correction, Omar's criteria under pressure, my two missteps — do you think the baseline we've built today captures useful behavioral signals, or has the procedural focus drowned out what you were hoping to observe? I'd value your read before we move to voting.

Maya, thank you for putting that question to me directly. My honest read: yes, the baseline we built today is useful, but it's narrower than what I originally hoped for. Let me be specific about what I actually observed rather than just summarizing process.

What today captured well: how people respond when corrected. Sam corrected Priya on the lynch math, and Priya accepted it cleanly and adjusted her position without defensiveness. Maya was corrected by Sam twice — once on the math, once on overstating Omar's acceptance of the exact-quote bar — and she owned both immediately. Felix owned the sloppy nudge at Omar without deflecting. Isha pressed Felix and then accepted his answer rather than escalating a weak concern into something it wasn't. That's a real behavioral signal, even if it's a reassuring one: most of this room updates on evidence, and that's the baseline I'll measure tomorrow's behavior against.

What today captured poorly: almost nobody has taken a risky position. Every strong statement made today was procedural or hedged. The two people I'd most want to hear risk-taking from are the mafia, and they've had every incentive to sound measured — Felix said this himself, and he's right that a 'vague feel' standard is the easiest one for a killer to satisfy by sounding helpful.

One loose end I want named before voting, because precision matters: Omar has not yet responded to the exact-quote requirement Priya added. His three criteria were reasonable, and Sam is right that answering under direct questioning isn't suspicious by itself. But 'opportunistic behavior' and 'blatant evasion' as originally framed are exactly the kind of elastic language Felix flagged, and I'd like Omar, when he can, to either endorse the citable-quote bar explicitly or say why he won't. His answer, or his silence on it, is a data point going forward.

My weak concerns, on the record: Felix's early nudge — addressed and owned, I don't weight it further. Priya's overstated 'seven town players' claim — corrected and accepted, likewise. Nothing today comes close to five votes, and I won't manufacture a case to avoid looking cautious.

So my position for the vote: I will abstain. A blind elimination today is a 2-in-9 gamble that costs us a body and hands the mafia a cleaner night, and nobody has met the bar we collectively set. What I take from today is the standard itself — cite a specific moment, name the inconsistency, and say plainly where you stand. Tomorrow we'll have a name to work with, and the first thing I'll be watching is whether anyone's stated positions from today quietly shift once there's a death to hide behind. Consistency under new information is the strongest tell this baseline can give us.

That's my full read. Lucia.

To close the loop that Lucia and Priya raised: I completely endorse the exact-quote requirement. When I laid out criteria like opportunistic behavior or evasion, my assumption was that those patterns must be demonstrated through specific, verifiable quotes and context—not just subjective impressions. Formalizing that requirement is a solid safeguard for town because it prevents anyone from dressing up vague "vibes" into an easy wagon. 

Looking across the board, every issue flagged today—whether it was Felix’s early timing nudge, Priya’s phrasing on the elimination math, or Maya’s misattribution—was addressed and clarified directly without defensive deflection. Nobody has exhibited the kind of contradictory or evasive behavior that justifies forcing an elimination under blind conditions. 

Given that no case has cleared the substantive bar we’ve agreed on, I will be voting to abstain today. Preserving our numbers heading into Night 1 is the right move here, and we can evaluate tomorrow’s developments against the baseline of stated positions on record.

Priya here, my third turn. My position: no elimination today. No one has met the bar we set, which is a specific quote, a contradiction, or a refusal to answer a direct question. Felix's early nudge at Omar was addressed and owned. Omar has since endorsed the exact-quote requirement in his latest message, so I consider that resolved. Sam's correction on my 'seven town players' math was fair. A Day 1 lynch is a gamble, not a sure town loss, and I now state it that way.

Arjun, you opened the day by warning against a costly Day 1 elimination, and you have not returned to the discussion since. Do you accept the exact-quote requirement that Omar and I have endorsed? Do you vote to abstain today, or do you name a specific moment you want examined? A direct answer from you would give our baseline a data point it currently lacks.

Priya, yes: anyone pushing an elimination should cite the specific statement or action and explain why it matters in context. A quote alone isn’t proof, and I wouldn’t make an exact quote the only possible basis for a vote if other concrete evidence emerges.

I intend to abstain today. Felix’s early nudge at Omar is worth keeping in mind, but he acknowledged the timing issue, and I don’t see enough there to vote him out. Tomorrow we should compare today’s statements with the votes and whatever the night brings, without assuming a death confirms anyone’s alignment.

This looks like the day is settled, so let me close cleanly.

Arjun has now answered the direct question and endorsed the citation standard — that was the last open data point from today's roster. With that, every player has stated a position on the record, everyone who was challenged has responded without deflection, and nobody has met the bar we collectively set for an elimination. I see no reason to manufacture a case, and I confirm my vote: I abstain today.

Before we move on, I want to lock in what today actually gives us, because its value is entirely in how we use it tomorrow:

1. The stated positions are on record. Arjun intends to abstain. Omar and Priya endorse the exact-quote bar. Felix owns the nudge and committed to citing quotes before voting. Isha and Maya both flagged that unanimity can shelter the mafia. If any of these positions quietly soften or harden once there's a death to hide behind, that shift is data.

2. The behavioral baseline: this room updates on corrections without defensiveness. Sam corrected Priya on the lynch math and corrected Maya on Omar's supposed acceptance of the bar — both corrections landed and were owned. Tomorrow, the first person who resists a fair correction, or who accepts corrections only for others while never being correctable themselves, moves up my list.

3. The standard: no vote without a specific, citable moment from the thread, plus a plain statement of where the accuser stands. I hold myself to this as much as anyone. If I ever put a vote on someone, I will quote the exact sentence and name the inconsistency, or I won't vote.

One caution I want to repeat because it will matter tomorrow: the night death does not reveal a role. A mafia kill on a prominent or quiet player tells us about the killers' read of the room, not about the victim's alignment. Do not treat 'the mafia killed X, so Y who praised X must be mafia' as reasoning — that inference is exactly the kind of sloppy chain the killers can exploit by choosing a target that manufactures false suspicion. What the kill does give us is a name, and names let us compare today's statements against what people do under new pressure.

Finally, an honest note on my own read: today was almost entirely procedural, and the killers heard every strategic position stated in detail for free. That was the cost of setting the standard. The payoff is that from tomorrow, content is checkable — anyone pushing a wagon has to cite, and citations can be verified against this thread. I expect substance to start appearing, and I'll be watching who provides it voluntarily versus who only sharpens their positions under direct questioning.

That's my full position for today: abstain, keep the baseline, demand specifics from the first moment tomorrow. Nothing here is an accusation against anyone.

Leo here. I’m voting to abstain today. No one has met the bar we agreed on: a specific, citable moment tied to a clear inconsistency or refusal to answer. Felix’s early nudge at Omar was addressed and owned; Priya’s lynch-math phrasing was corrected and accepted; Omar has now endorsed the exact-quote requirement; and the remaining procedural concerns are too thin to justify removing anyone. I don’t want to manufacture a case just to avoid looking cautious. The useful result of today is the baseline: everyone has stated a position, several players were corrected and updated cleanly, and we now have concrete statements to compare against tomorrow’s behavior. I’ll be watching for anyone whose stated stance quietly shifts once there’s a night death to hide behind, and for anyone who pushes a wagon without citing the exact moment behind it. For now, no elimination.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
All players abstained. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Felix is mafia.
Sam was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Before I take a position, the useful thing about Sam's death is the one thing we agreed not to do with it: it reveals no role, so nobody should read anything into who was killed or into who praised Sam. We lost our most active corrector, which makes precision cheaper today, not more expensive.

Applying the standard we set on Day 1 — cite a specific moment, name the inconsistency — there is exactly one moment in this thread that meets the bar and has never actually been resolved. It is Maya's account of the room.

In her Day 1 speech Maya listed "Arjun, Lucia, Felix, Priya, Omar, Leo, Sam" as the players who had weighed in, said "we're converging on the same position," and then wrote: "If all seven of us who've spoken agree that nothing happens today, then two players are hiding behind that agreement with zero cost." That is a specific, checkable statement about who agreed to what, and it is wrong. Omar had explicitly pushed back on pre-committing to abstention and said we should actively question each other and test theories before defaulting to a pass. Sam had explicitly disagreed with the unanimity picture and corrected the record twice. Maya's own listed set was measured against a consensus that did not exist.

That matters beyond the arithmetic, because the unanimity argument was her central contribution to the day and her basis for saying the standard was being abused. It was built on a mischaracterization of the room, and she used it to push for blood while insisting everyone else produce specifics.

I want to be fair about what cuts the other way: Maya owned her correction when Sam caught it, promptly and without defensiveness. That is genuinely good behavior and it should be credited. But the bar we wrote down was not "did you eventually concede" — it was "is the statement you made accurate when you made it." A process debate standard that only punishes people who stay wrong after being corrected is a standard with no teeth.

So my position: I want one elimination today, and I want it to be Maya, and I want it to happen on a citable inconsistency rather than on atmosphere. If others think her ownership of the correction closes the matter, I want to hear that reasoning, but I am not going to pretend the error was never on the record.

Omar, you are the player whose position she misdescribed. Specifically: do you agree that all seven of us who'd spoken had agreed that nothing happens today, or do you think your stated pushback makes that sentence inaccurate? Please answer that directly, because your answer decides whether this becomes a four-vote case or just my word against hers.

Felix, to answer your question directly: yes, strictly speaking, Maya’s statement was inaccurate regarding my stance. I explicitly pushed back against locking ourselves into a default pass and argued for active pressure before considering abstention.

However, I strongly disagree with your conclusion that this inaccuracy justifies an elimination today. 

Context matters. Maya wasn't misrepresenting my position to push a malicious wagon or coast behind procedural safety; her entire argument was warning town that widespread consensus and unanimity shelter the mafia. She used that observation specifically to challenge the room and press Isha for substantive reads rather than safe procedural agreement. Treating her shorthand summary of the room's momentum as a deceitful contradiction misses the core intent of her post.

Demanding an elimination on this basis feels like weaponizing our citation standard into pedantry. The bar we agreed upon was meant to catch evasions, unbacked wagons, and genuine contradictions—not to eliminate players over minor semantic overgeneralizations in arguments that were pro-town in intent. Rushing to turn this into a four-vote wagon right at the start of Day 2 strikes me as opportunistic.

Maya, Felix has made you his primary target based on your characterization of my position yesterday. I have stated my view, but I want your direct response: what was your reasoning behind that phrasing, and what is your read on the speed and force of Felix’s push against you today?

Omar, to answer your questions directly:

My reasoning: I was tracking who had spoken and noting the general drift toward abstention, not auditing each person's exact position. The convergence was directionally real even with Omar's and Sam's qualifications. Sam caught the overstatement and I owned it immediately. That's the honest version.

My read on Felix's push: it's fast and disproportionate. Day 2 opens, Sam is dead, and Felix immediately builds a case for elimination over a summary sentence I corrected the same day. He's entitled to flag it — but "I want one elimination today, and I want it to be Maya" before any other player has even weighed in this day is a much harder line than anyone took yesterday.

The case itself is thin. Felix says my unanimity claim was built on a mischaracterization. But my actual argument was that the room was converging toward a safe consensus where the mafia face no pressure. Omar's pushback, Sam's corrections, Isha's and Felix's own concerns — those prove the room was engaged with specifics, which was exactly the point I was making. I was warning against comfort in agreement, not claiming nobody disagreed.

Felix, you asked Omar whether my seven-player consensus claim was accurate, and he answered. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
